tasks.short: Read the dispatch details, examine the patient and take vital signs, decide and prioritise procedures, record findings and check the national protocol.

steps.what: Ambulance crew member reads the dispatch details on the way
Ambulance crew member examines the patient to assess the nature and extent of illness or injury
Ambulance crew member decides and prioritizes medical procedures
Ambulance crew member writes vital signs and findings on the patient form
Ambulance crew member checks the national protocol for the condition

tasks.design: The monitor sends vital signs with times to the electronic patient form on the ambulance tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}), so only findings need entering. The national ambulance protocol is on the same tablet with search by complaint. Examining, deciding and prioritising stay with the crew; no AI triages.
tasks.previous_blocker: Vitals were written down from the monitor and the protocol looked up in a booklet.
tasks.enabler_now: Ambulance monitors export vitals to electronic patient forms.
tasks.still_hard: On scene there is often no time to look anything up.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a quiet patient is in more danger than a loud one.

evidence.claim: Ambulance monitors export vital signs to electronic patient forms.
Reserved acts may be done by others only on assignment with instructions.

assumptions: Boundary: from the dispatch call to protocol steps; treatment itself is outside.
Input contract: vitals from the ambulance monitor; protocol from the national ambulance protocol body; fallback is writing down.
Examining and deciding do not change.

incremental.description: Ambulance crew member checks the monitor link at shift start.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: older monitors without a link, so most vitals are still written (s4 keeps 80), and protocol search helps little (s5 keeps 85) (4.0); high: linked monitors and the protocol on the tablet (11.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: See which certifications are due, sign up for classes, attend training and skill tests, study e-learning and protocol updates and hand in certificates.

steps.what: Ambulance crew member checks which certifications are due
Ambulance crew member e-mails the training office to sign up for classes
Ambulance crew member attends training classes to maintain certification
Ambulance crew member studies e-learning and protocol updates
Instructors record skill tests and completed modules in the learning system
Ambulance crew member hands in certificates to the training office: all on paper today, only certificates from outside courses after the change

tasks.design: The learning system ({LMS}) shows each crew member's certifications with expiry dates and lets them book classes themselves. Instructors record skill tests and completed modules there, so certificates no longer need handing in. Training, skill tests and study stay with the crew member.
tasks.previous_blocker: Expiry dates were kept in spreadsheets and certificates handed in on paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning systems track certifications and record results from instructors.
tasks.still_hard: Rosters make it hard to attend classes; planning still needs a person.
tasks.human_edge: Practising a difficult airway until it is automatic.

evidence.claim: Learning systems track certifications with expiry dates and record instructors' results.
Records of employee test results can count as staff monitoring, so the works council must consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from certification dates to the certification record; rostering is outside.
Input contract: results entered by instructors; fallback is paper certificates.
Training and study do not change.
Instructors record results (s4i) in about the time signing a certificate took; their time is outside the crew member's savings. s5 keeps 10 for certificates from outside courses.

already_counted.description: Ambulance crew member reads the expiry list.

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: the training office keeps the learning system; learning the booking screen is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: expiry dates are often missing (s1 keeps 60), classes are still booked by e-mail (s2 keeps 80) and many certificates come from outside courses (s5 keeps 50) (9.5); high: the learning system holds all certifications (18.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Talk calmly with the patient during care, explain what happens next, reassure family at the scene and give them the hospital details.

steps.what: Ambulance crew member comforts and reassures patients during care
Ambulance crew member explains to the patient what will happen next
Ambulance crew member reassures family members at the scene
Ambulance crew member writes the hospital name and phone number on a note for the family

tasks.design: The ambulance tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}) prints a small card with the destination hospital's name, address and phone number for the family, so the crew does not write it by hand. Comforting, explaining and reassuring stay with the crew.
tasks.previous_blocker: Hospital details were written on scraps of paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Ambulance tablets can print short notes.
tasks.still_hard: Families need a calm person, not a card.
tasks.human_edge: Holding a frightened child's hand during the ride.

reach.learn: Whether cards cut calls to the wrong hospital.

evidence.claim: Ambulance tablets can print short notes from the ride record.
Health data are special category data; the card shows only the hospital, not the condition.

assumptions: Boundary: from care at the scene to the family note; transport is outside.
Input contract: destination chosen by the crew with dispatch; fallback is writing by hand.
Comforting and reassuring do not change.
No patient details go on the card.
unknowns: Rides with family at the scene.
research_questions: Do families reach the right hospital more often?

incremental.description: Ambulance crew member refills the card printer.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the printer is often out of order, so most notes are still written (s4 keeps 80) (0.8); high: cards printed on most rides (2.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Report status to dispatch, complete findings for handover, pass the pre-arrival report to the hospital, ask for treatment instructions and hand over the patient.

steps.what: Ambulance crew member reports arrival and status to dispatchers by radio
Ambulance crew member completes findings and vital signs for the handover
Ambulance crew member checks the final pre-arrival report: vitals and findings against the patient, and the receiving emergency department
Ambulance crew member sends the pre-arrival report to the hospital: read out by phone today, released once to the emergency department's screen after the change
Ambulance crew member asks the physician for further treatment instructions
Ambulance crew member hands over the patient in person at the emergency department

tasks.design: Status buttons on the ambulance tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}) replace most radio status calls and record times. The handover report fills from the monitor and the crew's findings; the crew checks the final report and its destination and releases it once to the receiving emergency department's screen before arrival. Asking for instructions and the handover in person stay with the crew; critical patients still get a short call.
tasks.previous_blocker: Status and pre-arrival reports were given by radio and phone.
tasks.enabler_now: Ambulance systems send structured reports to emergency departments.
tasks.still_hard: Receiving hospitals use different systems; some still need a call.
tasks.human_edge: Telling the trauma team in ten seconds what they need to know.

reach.learn: Whether written pre-arrival reports improve preparation.

evidence.claim: Ambulance systems can send structured pre-arrival reports to emergency departments.
Medical data must be shared securely; fax is banned for sharing.

assumptions: Boundary: from ride status to the patient handed over; hospital treatment is outside.
Input contract: vitals from the monitor; destination from dispatch; fallback is radio and phone.

Instructions, the in-person handover and the report check keep their full time. s1 keeps 30 because status buttons replace most radio calls; s2 keeps 60 because vitals fill from the monitor and the crew writes the findings; s3 keeps 5 for the release.
Hospital staff's time is outside the crew's savings.
research_questions: Does handover time at the door fall?

already_counted.description: Ambulance crew member checks the handover report.

incremental.description: Ambulance crew member phones about critical patients.

approvals.approved_version: The pre-arrival report with vitals and findings exactly as checked by the crew in s2c, sent once to the screen of the receiving emergency department; changes need a new check before sending.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: crews keep using the radio for status (s1 keeps 60) and many departments still want a phone report (s3 keeps 40) (23.4); high: status buttons and screen reports in use (36.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The ambulance crew member keeps assessment, care, comfort and handover; writing vitals, radio calls and paper certificates shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A crew that arrives with the hospital already prepared.
